Withholding and CAT have no filing deadline
counter_arguments: Mere awareness of right to apply is not extraordinary circumstance
Delay after circumstances change may defeat reasonableness
Burden is on applicant — conclusory assertions insufficient
doctrines.applicability_test: Query involves asylum one-year filing deadline, exceptions to one-year bar, late-filed asylum, changed or extraordinary circumstances.

doctrines.conclusion_template: INA §320 provides automatic citizenship to children born abroad who: (1) have at least one USC parent; (2) child is under 18; (3) child is LPR; (4) child is residing in US in legal and physical custody of USC parent. Effective February 27, 2001 (Child Citizenship Act). INA §322 allows USC parent to apply for naturalization of child residing abroad if parent has 5 years physical presence in US (2 after age 14). For children born abroad to USC parents: INA §301/§309 govern citizenship at birth.
doctrines.reasoning_framework:
1. INA §320 AUTOMATIC: All four requirements met simultaneously → automatic citizenship. No application required but can obtain certificate of citizenship (N-600).
2. INA §322 APPLICATION: For children of USCs residing abroad. Parent applies. Child must be under 18, temporarily present in US for oath.
3. INA §301 BIRTH ABROAD: Citizenship at birth if (a) both parents USCs with one having US residence; (b) one USC parent with 5 years physical presence (2 after age 14) before child's birth.
4. INA §309 OUT-OF-WEDLOCK: Additional requirements for unwed USC fathers — written agreement to support, legitimation, paternity established by court.
5. RETROACTIVITY: CCA applies to children who were under 18 on 2/27/2001 AND met all requirements simultaneously.
6. DOCUMENTATION: N-600 (Certificate of Citizenship) or US passport as evidence.
key_factors: INA §320: automatic if all 4 requirements met simultaneously while child under 18
INA §322: application for child abroad — parent must have 5 years US presence
INA §301: citizenship at birth abroad to USC parents
Child Citizenship Act effective 2/27/2001
Proof via N-600 or US passport application

primary_authority.reference: Child Citizenship Act of 2000, Pub. L. 106-395

counter_arguments: All four §320 requirements must be met simultaneously while child under 18
Adoption cases require final adoption — not mere custody
Physical presence requirements for §301 must be documented precisely
doctrines.applicability_test: Query involves derivative citizenship, automatic citizenship for children, Child Citizenship Act, INA §320, or citizenship at birth abroad.

doctrines.conclusion_template: INA §212(a)(9)(A) bars admission of previously removed aliens: 5 years after removal, 10 years after removal if second removal or if convicted of aggravated felony, 20 years after second or subsequent removal. INA §212(a)(9)(C) imposes permanent bar for aliens with 1+ year unlawful presence who reenter without inspection. I-212 application for consent to reapply before expiration of statutory bar period. Discretionary — weighs basis for removal, recency, moral character, family ties, need for services.
doctrines.reasoning_framework:
1. §212(a)(9)(A) BARS: (i) 5 years for removal/exclusion/VD-in-lieu; (ii) 10 years for removal order, second or subsequent removal, or aggravated felony; (iii) 20 years for second or subsequent removal.
2. §212(a)(9)(C) PERMANENT BAR: 1+ year unlawful presence then reentry/attempted reentry without inspection. Only waivable after 10 years outside US via I-212 + consent from Secretary.
3. I-212 APPLICATION: Filed to seek consent to reapply before bar period expires.
4. DISCRETIONARY FACTORS: Basis for prior removal, recency, moral character, respect for law, family ties, business/property ties, community ties, need for alien's services.
5. TIMING: Can file I-212 from abroad or, in limited circumstances, from within US.
6. NOT AUTOMATIC: Approval of I-212 does not guarantee admission — still must overcome all other inadmissibility grounds.
key_factors: 5/10/20 year bars depending on removal history
Permanent bar under §212(a)(9)(C) for unlawful reentry
I-212 consent is discretionary
Approval does not guarantee admission
Must also overcome any other inadmissibility grounds
counter_arguments: Filing I-212 alone does not overcome other inadmissibility grounds
§212(a)(9)(C) permanent bar extremely difficult to overcome — requires 10 years outside US first
Aggravated felony prior removal may make I-212 discretionary denial likely
doctrines.applicability_test: Query involves reentry after removal, I-212, consent to reapply, post-removal bars, or permanent reentry bar.

doctrines.conclusion_template: INA §249 allows adjustment to LPR status for aliens who: (1) entered the US before January 1, 1972; (2) have continuously resided in US since entry; (3) are persons of good moral character; (4) are not inadmissible under §212(a)(3)(E) (Nazi persecution) or §212(a)(2) to extent they are ineligible for citizenship; (5) are not subject to removal as deportable. Filed on Form I-485 with evidence of pre-1972 entry and continuous residence.
doctrines.reasoning_framework:
1. ENTRY DATE: Must have entered US before January 1, 1972. Manner of entry irrelevant — EWI qualifies.
2. CONTINUOUS RESIDENCE: Since entry. Brief, casual, and innocent absences permitted.
3. GOOD MORAL CHARACTER: Must demonstrate GMC — statutory bars in INA §101(f) apply.
4. ADMISSIBILITY: Not inadmissible under §212(a)(3)(E) (Nazi persecution). Criminal grounds may apply if rendering ineligible for citizenship.
5. NOT DEPORTABLE: Cannot be subject to removal under deportability grounds.
6. EVIDENCE: Any credible evidence of pre-1972 entry — school records, employment records, tax records, church records, affidavits.
7. DISCRETIONARY: Grant is discretionary even if all statutory requirements met.
key_factors: Entry before January 1, 1972
Manner of entry irrelevant — EWI qualifies
Continuous residence since entry
Good moral character required
Any credible evidence of entry date accepted

primary_authority.reference: USCIS Policy Manual Vol. 7, Pt. L

counter_arguments: Registry date has not been updated since 1986 — increasingly rare applicant pool
Continuous residence burden is on applicant
Criminal grounds may bar even if entry date established
doctrines.applicability_test: Query involves registry, INA §249, pre-1972 entry, or long-term resident adjustment under registry provisions.

doctrines.conclusion_template: Parole in place grants parole to individuals already present in the US, providing inspected and paroled status that satisfies AOS eligibility under INA §245(a) without requiring physical departure. Established by regulation and policy — available for military families (spouses, parents, children of active duty/veterans) and periodically expanded by executive action. PIP resolves the EWI bar to AOS by providing paroled status deemed equivalent to inspection and admission.
doctrines.reasoning_framework:
1. PURPOSE: Allows EWI aliens to be paroled without departing, satisfying I&A/P requirement for AOS.
2. MILITARY PIP: Established authority for spouses, parents, and children of active duty military, veterans, and deceased service members.
3. HUMANITARIAN PIP: Discretionary DHS authority under INA §212(d)(5)(A) for urgent humanitarian reasons or significant public benefit.
4. PROCESS: Apply via I-131 (Application for Travel Document) or pursuant to specific program guidance.
5. EFFECT: Recipient is deemed inspected and paroled. May proceed with AOS (I-485) if otherwise eligible.
6. NOT STATUS: Parole is not an immigration status — does not prevent removal proceedings.
7. DURATION: Set by DHS at time of grant. May be revoked.
key_factors: Resolves EWI bar to adjustment of status
Military families have established eligibility
Does not confer immigration status
Discretionary — no entitlement
Must still meet all other AOS requirements

primary_authority.reference: USCIS Policy Manual Vol. 7, Pt. B, Ch. 4

counter_arguments: PIP programs subject to executive policy changes — may be expanded or curtailed
Parole can be revoked at any time before AOS approval
PIP does not cure other inadmissibility grounds — separate waivers may be needed
doctrines.applicability_test: Query involves parole in place, PIP for military families, humanitarian parole, or resolving EWI for adjustment purposes.

doctrines.conclusion_template: INA §204(j) (per AC21 §106) allows employment-based I-485 applicants to change employers or positions after I-485 has been pending 180+ days, provided new job is in same or similar occupational classification. I-140 remains valid even if original employer withdraws (if I-485 pending 180+ days). Applicant retains priority date. No new PERM or I-140 required for portability — just demonstrate same/similar.
doctrines.reasoning_framework:
1. ELIGIBILITY: I-485 pending 180+ days. Employment-based category.
2. SAME OR SIMILAR: New position must be in same or similar occupational classification as original I-140 job. Per USCIS guidance — SOC code comparison is useful but not determinative.
3. I-140 VALIDITY: I-140 remains valid for portability even if employer withdraws/revokes AFTER I-485 pending 180 days.
4. NOTIFICATION: File Supplement J to I-485 to notify USCIS of new employer/position.
5. NO NEW PERM: No new labor certification required — portability preserves original PERM/I-140.
6. PRIORITY DATE RETENTION: Original priority date retained regardless of employer change.
7. EAD: Use EAD (c)(9) to work for new employer during I-485 pendency.
key_factors: I-485 must be pending 180+ days
Same or similar occupational classification
I-140 survives employer withdrawal after 180-day mark
No new PERM or I-140 needed
Priority date retained across employer changes

primary_authority.relevance: American Competitiveness in the 21st Century Act

counter_arguments: Same or similar determination is fact-specific — significant deviation from original job may disqualify
If I-140 revoked for fraud/misrepresentation, portability does not apply
Must actually intend to work in offered position at time of AOS approval
doctrines.applicability_test: Query involves AC21 portability, changing employers during green card process, same or similar occupation, or I-485 job change.

doctrines.conclusion_template: INA §240A(b)(2) provides cancellation of removal for battered spouses/children/parents of USCs or LPRs. Requirements: (1) battered or subjected to extreme cruelty by USC/LPR spouse or parent; (2) 3 years continuous physical presence; (3) good moral character during 3-year period; (4) removal would result in extreme hardship to alien, alien's child, or alien's parent. Lower hardship standard than non-LPR cancellation. Not subject to 4,000 annual cap.
doctrines.reasoning_framework:
1. QUALIFYING ABUSE: Battery or extreme cruelty by USC or LPR spouse or parent. Must establish connection between abuse and immigration situation.
2. 3-YEAR PRESENCE: Continuous physical presence for 3 years (not 10 as in regular non-LPR cancellation).
3. GMC: Good moral character during 3-year period. VAWA provisions may excuse certain conduct connected to abuse.
4. HARDSHIP: Extreme hardship (not exceptional and extremely unusual) to alien, child, or parent. Lower standard than §240A(b)(1).
5. NO CAP: Not subject to 4,000 annual grant limitation.
6. SELF-PETITION NOT REQUIRED: Can seek VAWA cancellation even without prior self-petition.
7. CONFIDENTIALITY: Full VAWA confidentiality protections apply per INA §384.
key_factors: 3 years physical presence (not 10)
Extreme hardship standard (lower than non-LPR cancellation)
Hardship to alien themselves counts — not just qualifying relative
Not subject to 4,000 annual cap
VAWA confidentiality protections apply
counter_arguments: Must establish abuse by USC or LPR — abuse by non-qualifying person insufficient
GMC requirement may be affected by criminal history unrelated to abuse
Alien must demonstrate causal connection between abuse and immigration situation
doctrines.applicability_test: Query involves VAWA cancellation of removal, battered spouse cancellation, INA §240A(b)(2), or abuse-based relief in removal proceedings.

doctrines.conclusion_template: Advance parole (AP) under INA §212(d)(5) allows alien to travel abroad and return to US without abandoning pending I-485 or other applications. Filed on Form I-131. Critical: departing without AP while I-485 pending generally results in deemed abandonment of AOS. AP combined with EAD on combo card for AOS applicants. Returning on AP = paroled, not admitted — may affect certain immigration consequences.
doctrines.reasoning_framework:
1. WHO NEEDS AP: I-485 pending applicants, TPS holders, DACA recipients, deferred action recipients who wish to travel.
2. DEEMED ABANDONMENT: Departing without AP while I-485 pending = abandonment unless H-1B/L-1 (dual intent) or H-4/L-2 in some circumstances.
3. COMBO CARD: EAD/AP combination card issued to I-485 applicants. Functions as both work authorization and travel document.
4. REENTRY PERMIT: For LPRs planning extended absence (1+ year). Filed on I-131 while in US. Valid 2 years.
5. PAROLE VS ADMISSION: Returning on AP = paroled. Implications for inadmissibility analysis — full §212(a) grounds apply.
6. CONDITIONAL: AP grant is discretionary. May be revoked.
7. VALIDITY: Typically 1 year from issuance. Must be valid at time of reentry.
key_factors: Required for travel during pending I-485 (unless H-1B/L-1 dual intent)
Departure without AP = deemed abandonment of AOS
Combo card combines EAD and AP
Return on AP = paroled status, not admitted
Reentry permit for LPRs traveling 1+ year
counter_arguments: H-1B/L-1 holders can depart and return on valid visa without AP per dual intent
TPS AP travel creates admission per some circuits — may cure prior EWI
Emergency AP available for unforeseen circumstances
doctrines.applicability_test: Query involves advance parole, travel during pending green card application, I-131, reentry permit, or travel document requirements.

doctrines.conclusion_template: Controlled substance offenses create severe immigration consequences. Inadmissibility: INA §212(a)(2)(A)(i)(II) — conviction or admission of violation of controlled substance law. Deportability: INA §237(a)(2)(B)(i) — conviction of CS violation other than single offense involving 30g or less of marijuana for personal use. Drug trafficking aggravated felony per §101(a)(43)(B). Only limited waivers available — §212(h) waiver available for single offense of simple possession of 30g or less marijuana.
doctrines.reasoning_framework:
1. INADMISSIBILITY §212(a)(2)(A)(i)(II): Convicted of or admits violating any law relating to controlled substance. Includes mere admission without conviction.
2. DEPORTABILITY §237(a)(2)(B)(i): Convicted of violation. Single offense of 30g marijuana for personal use excepted.
3. AGGRAVATED FELONY: Drug trafficking per §101(a)(43)(B) — includes distribution, even social sharing may qualify per Moncrieffe analysis.
4. WAIVER LIMITATIONS: §212(h) waiver only for single offense of simple possession of 30g or less marijuana. No other CS waivers for inadmissibility.
5. REASON TO BELIEVE: §212(a)(2)(C) — known or believed to be illicit trafficker. No conviction required — reasonable suspicion standard.
6. STATE LEGALIZATION: Federal immigration law controls — state marijuana legalization irrelevant for immigration purposes.
7. PARAPHERNALIA: Some states' paraphernalia convictions may not be CS violation if statute broader than CSA.
key_factors: Admission alone (without conviction) can trigger inadmissibility
Only single offense 30g marijuana has waiver/exception
State marijuana legalization irrelevant for immigration
Drug trafficking = aggravated felony with severe consequences
Reason to believe trafficker — no conviction needed
counter_arguments: State paraphernalia statute may be overbroad — not matching federal CSA = categorical mismatch
Post-conviction relief may eliminate CS conviction in some jurisdictions/circuits
Admission must be voluntary and without duress to trigger inadmissibility
doctrines.applicability_test: Query involves controlled substance convictions, drug offenses and immigration, marijuana and immigration, or drug trafficking immigration consequences.

doctrines.conclusion_template: INA §237(a)(2)(E) provides specific deportability grounds for domestic violence, stalking, child abuse/neglect/abandonment, and violation of protection order. Conviction of crime of domestic violence (as defined in 18 USC §16 applied to intimate partner) renders deportable. Stalking conviction deportable. Child abuse/neglect/abandonment conviction deportable. Violation of protection order deportable if involves protection against credible threats, repeated harassment, or bodily injury.
doctrines.reasoning_framework:
1. DOMESTIC VIOLENCE §237(a)(2)(E)(i): Convicted of crime of domestic violence as defined — crime of violence (18 USC §16) committed against current/former spouse, cohabitant, person sharing child, person similarly situated under domestic/family violence laws.
2. STALKING §237(a)(2)(E)(i): Convicted of stalking offense.
3. CHILD ABUSE §237(a)(2)(E)(i): Convicted of child abuse, child neglect, or child abandonment.
4. PROTECTION ORDER §237(a)(2)(E)(ii): Determined to have violated protection order that involves protection against credible threats of violence, repeated harassment, or bodily injury.
5. CRIME OF VIOLENCE: Per 18 USC §16 — use/attempted use/threatened use of physical force OR substantial risk that force may be used in committing. Per Sessions v. Dimaya — §16(b) void for vagueness, only §16(a) valid.
6. NO WAIVER: No specific statutory waiver for DV deportability ground. Cancellation of removal may be only relief (if no aggravated felony).
key_factors: Crime of violence against intimate partner = deportable
Protection order violation deportable even without conviction
Sessions v. Dimaya eliminated §16(b) — only §16(a) valid
No specific waiver for DV deportability ground
VAWA protections available for victims — not perpetrators
counter_arguments: Under Dimaya, only §16(a) element — use/attempted use/threatened use of physical force — remains valid
Not all state DV convictions match federal crime of violence definition
Protection order violation must meet specific statutory requirements — mere civil order violation insufficient

doctrines.conclusion_template: INA §240(c)(6) allows one motion to reconsider within 30 days based on legal errors. INA §240(c)(7) allows one motion to reopen within 90 days based on new facts/evidence not available at prior hearing. Exceptions to time/number limits: changed country conditions (asylum claims, no time limit), ineffective assistance of counsel, VAWA (no time/number limits for DV victims), sua sponte (IJ/BIA discretion). In absentia orders: rescission within 180 days (failure to receive notice) or any time (lack of proper notice or exceptional circumstances).
doctrines.reasoning_framework:
1. RECONSIDERATION §240(c)(6): One motion, within 30 days. Must specify errors of law or fact. No new evidence.
2. REOPENING §240(c)(7): One motion, within 90 days. Must present previously unavailable material evidence likely to change outcome.
3. EXCEPTIONS TO TIME/NUMBER LIMITS:
   a. Changed country conditions — no time limit for asylum/withholding/CAT claims
   b. Ineffective assistance per Matter of Lozada — must show: attorney retained, notified of complaint, prejudice
   c. VAWA — no time or number limits for abuse victims
   d. Joint DHS-alien motion — no time limit
   e. Sua sponte — BIA/IJ discretion, no time limit
4. IN ABSENTIA: §240(b)(5)(C) — rescission within 180 days for lack of receipt, or any time for failure to provide proper notice or exceptional circumstances.
5. STAY OF REMOVAL: Filing MTR does not automatically stay removal. Must file separate motion for stay.
6. DEPARTURE BAR: Generally cannot reopen after departure except for in absentia rescission in some circuits.
key_factors: One motion to reconsider (30 days) and one to reopen (90 days)
Changed country conditions exception — no time limit
Lozada requirements for IAC claims
Filing does not automatically stay removal
Departure generally bars reopening
counter_arguments: Sua sponte authority is broad but rarely exercised — not a guaranteed path
Changed country conditions must be material to the specific claim
Departure bar has circuit-level exceptions that should be analyzed
